aeo.what_is: Food restriction due to sensory issues, fear of eating consequences, or low appetite—not weight concerns.

content.description: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is characterized by an eating or feeding disturbance leading to persistent failure to meet appropriate nutritional and/or energy needs, associated with one or more of: significant weight loss or faltering growth, significant nutritional deficiency, dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements, and marked interference with psychosocial functioning. Unlike anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, ARFID is not driven by body weight/shape concerns.
content.temporal_criteria: ARFID requires persistent eating disturbance (not transient or acute) with failure to meet nutritional/energy needs. No specific minimum duration is mandated, but patterns must be ongoing rather than brief reactions to illness or stress. Remission requires resolution of nutritional compromise and psychosocial interference. Severity is determined by degree of medical risk, nutritional deficiency, and functional impairment.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: ARFID is often missed because it's dismissed as 'picky eating' or attributed solely to behavioral defiance, especially in children. Providers may focus on treating GI symptoms (reflux, constipation) without recognizing that anxiety or sensory issues maintain the avoidance. ARFID can be confused with anorexia nervosa when weight loss occurs, but the key distinction is the absence of body image disturbance or fear of weight gain. It can also be mistaken for autism-related feeding selectivity when sensory issues are present, but ARFID requires significant nutritional or psychosocial impairment. The disorder is underrecognized in adolescents and adults who maintain normal weight but rely heavily on supplements or have marked functional interference.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Eating/feeding disturbance (e.g., apparent lack of interest in eating/food; avoidance based on sensory characteristics; concern about aversive consequences of eating) leading to persistent failure to meet nutritional/energy needs associated with ≥1 of: 1) significant weight loss or faltering growth; 2) significant nutritional deficiency; 3) dependence on enteral feeding or oral supplements; 4) marked psychosocial interference. B. Not better explained by lack of available food or culturally sanctioned practice. C. Not occurring exclusively during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa and no disturbance in body weight/shape perception. D. Not attributable to a concurrent medical condition or better explained by another mental disorder; if present, the severity of eating disturbance exceeds that routinely associated with the condition.
content.prevalence: Estimated ~1–5% in pediatric populations; increasingly recognized in adolescents and adults. Often underdiagnosed when weight is normal.
content.age_of_onset: Frequently begins in early childhood; can emerge or persist into adolescence/adulthood.
content.prognosis: Variable course. Many improve with exposure-based therapies and multidisciplinary care; chronicity risk increases with longstanding sensory aversions, severe anxiety, or medical comorbidities. Early intervention reduces growth and psychosocial impact.

circuitry: Heightened salience and sensory processing differences (insula, somatosensory cortex) linked to taste/texture/odor sensitivity.
Threat and interoceptive circuits (amygdala–insula) implicated in fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype (e.g., choking, vomiting).
Reduced reward responsivity to food cues and altered interoceptive awareness in the low-interest subtype.
psychophysiology: Elevated anxiety/arousal to food cues (HR, skin conductance) in fear-based presentations.
Gastrointestinal sensation–perception mismatch (visceral hypersensitivity) may maintain avoidance.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Familial anxiety/neurodevelopmental traits (ASD/ADHD) and early adverse feeding experiences (choking, severe emesis) increase risk.

history_psychosocial: Detailed feeding history: onset, growth trajectory, preferred/avoided foods, textures, temperatures, colors, smells.
Precipitating events (e.g., choking, emesis, anaphylaxis), mealtime routines, duration of meals, distress level.
Functional impact: school/work interference, family conflict, social eating avoidance.
medical_assessment: Vitals (orthostatic HR/BP), weight/BMI with growth curves; hydration status.
Labs guided by intake: CBC, CMP, magnesium, phosphorus, calcium; iron studies, vitamin D, B12/folate, zinc; consider thyroid studies.
Monitor refeeding risk when intake increases (phosphorus, potassium, magnesium).
feeding_swallowing_assessment: Speech-language pathology or occupational therapy evaluation for oral-motor skills, sensory processing, and swallow safety.
Videofluoroscopic swallow study if aspiration risk or persistent fear of choking despite normal exam.
GI_and_allergy_workup: Screen for GERD, eosinophilic esophagitis, celiac disease, constipation, and food allergies when suggested by history.
Treat medical contributors while continuing behavioral therapy.
standardized_measures: PARDI or NIAS for ARFID profiles; EDE-Q as adjunct (expect low weight/shape concern scores).
SCARED/GAD-7/PHQ-9 for anxiety/depression; sensory profiles where relevant.
risk_stratification: Hospitalization/urgent thresholds similar to other restrictive disorders: unstable vitals (e.g., HR <50 adolescents/<40 adults; symptomatic orthostasis), electrolyte abnormalities, syncope, acute food refusal, rapid weight loss, inability to maintain outpatient intake, suicidality.
differential_diagnosis: Feeding difficulties in ASD without significant nutritional/functional impairment.
GI disorders causing pain/nausea without primary fear/avoidance maintenance.
Food insecurity or culturally sanctioned dietary practices.
evaluation.team_and_process: Multidisciplinary care (medical, therapist with ARFID expertise, dietitian; SLP/OT as indicated). Collaborate with school/college dining and family.

profiles: Sensory sensitivity: avoidance based on texture, taste, smell, temperature, or appearance.
Fear of aversive consequences: avoidance due to fear of choking, vomiting, allergic reaction, abdominal pain.
Apparent lack of interest: low appetite, early satiety, limited hunger cues, forgetting to eat.
impact_examples: Very limited accepted foods (e.g., only beige/crunchy foods).
Prolonged meals with distress; avoidance of cafeterias/restaurants.
Reliance on supplements or tube feeds to meet nutritional needs.
physical: Faltering growth/weight loss (not required if psychosocial impact is marked).
Fatigue, dizziness, cold intolerance; micronutrient deficiencies (iron, zinc, B12, vitamin D).
GI symptoms (constipation, early satiety, nausea) that may both cause and result from low intake.

severity_levels.mild: Narrow diet without significant medical compromise; psychosocial interference limited.
severity_levels.moderate: Nutritional deficiency and/or reliance on supplements; notable family/school impact.
severity_levels.severe: Weight/growth compromise or medical instability; dependence on enteral feeds; marked psychosocial impairment.

biological: History of prematurity or early feeding problems
Family history of anxiety, ASD, or GI disorders
psychological: High trait anxiety and harm avoidance
environmental: Negative mealtime dynamics or high-pressure feeding
Food allergy experiences; restricted access to preferred foods

impact_on_life.home: Conflict and prolonged mealtimes; caregiver stress.
impact_on_life.medical: Micronutrient deficiencies; constipation; delayed growth/puberty in youth.

comorbidities: GI conditions (GERD, functional abdominal pain, EoE)

psychotherapy: CBT-AR (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for ARFID): psychoeducation, nutritional rehabilitation, graded exposure to feared/sensory foods, interoceptive exposure, and relapse prevention.
Family-Based Treatment for ARFID (FBT-ARFID) with caregiver-led support and reduction of accommodation/pressure cycles.
Exposure-based feeding therapy with SLP/OT for oral-sensory desensitization and skill-building.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) elements for values-based eating and anxiety tolerance.
nutrition_rehabilitation: Dietitian-guided expansion plan targeting energy needs and micronutrients.
Use of oral supplements strategically; taper as food variety increases.
Enteral feeding when medically necessary with parallel exposure to maintain oral intake.
medical_management: Treat GI contributors (constipation regimen, reflux management).
Monitor vitals, growth, and labs; manage refeeding risk during intake increases.
medications: Appetite/anxiety support (adjunctive): cyproheptadine for appetite and gastric accommodation (pediatrics, off-label); mirtazapine for appetite, anxiety, and sleep; SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) for comorbid anxiety/OCD; hydroxyzine short-term for meal-related anxiety or nausea.
Avoid bupropion in patients with significant weight loss or purging risk.
Use antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron) short-term to facilitate exposure in fear-of-vomiting subtype when clinically indicated.
school_college_supports: 504/IEP accommodations (flexible meal times/locations, access to preferred starter foods, refrigeration/microwave).
Meal support plans and coordination with dining services.
lifestyle_interventions: Regular meal/snack schedule with low-pressure exposure practice.
Sleep hygiene and gentle physical activity to support appetite and GI motility.
Family coaching on neutral language and reinforcement of approach behaviors.

treatment_goals: Restore adequate nutrition, growth, and medical stability.
Increase variety and volume of foods across textures and contexts.
Reduce avoidance, fear, and distress around eating via graded exposure.
Improve psychosocial participation (school, work, social meals).
Taper reliance on supplements/enteral feeds when safe.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Normal BMI masking significant nutritional deficiency and psychosocial interference.
Labeled as 'picky eating' without assessing growth, micronutrients, or distress.
Presentation framed solely as GI disorder; ARFID not considered after negative workup.
Assuming avoidance is behavioral noncompliance rather than anxiety/sensory driven.
overdiagnosis_factors: Selective eating without nutritional deficiency or psychosocial impairment.
Dieting with body-image concerns (should suggest anorexia/bulimia spectrum instead).
Culturally/religiously restricted diets misinterpreted as psychopathology.
Food insecurity or limited access driving intake patterns.

specifiers.note: Specify primary profile(s) to guide exposure hierarchy and team composition (e.g., SLP/OT involvement for sensory/swallow issues).

warning_signs: Rapid reduction in variety/volume of accepted foods.
Dizziness/syncope, cold intolerance, or signs of micronutrient deficiency (pallor, brittle hair/nails).
Meal-related panic or refusal after a choking/vomiting event.
Dependence on supplements/tube feeds without parallel oral intake work.
self_help_strategies: Track accepted foods and build a gradual exposure ladder (one new food step at a time).
Pair new foods with familiar flavors/textures; use tiny bites with timed practice.
Practice interoceptive awareness (noticing hunger/fullness) and paced breathing before meals.
Caregivers: reduce pressure/negotiation; praise approach behaviors and time-at-table rather than bites alone.

early_childhood: Strong texture/temperature selectivity; prolonged meals; distress with new foods.
Parent coaching, SLP/OT feeding therapy, and low-pressure exposure are key.
school_age: Lunch avoidance, field trip challenges; reliance on packed 'safe' foods.
CBT-AR modules with school coordination and micronutrient monitoring.
adolescence: Social eating avoidance; nutritional deficits impacting sports/academics.
Family-supported exposures, autonomy-building, and anxiety treatment.
adulthood: Work travel/meals stressful; limited cuisine flexibility.
CBT-AR adapted for adults; dietitian plans for variety and nutrition sufficiency.

first_person_statements: People think I'm just picky, but trying new foods triggers intense anxiety and gagging. It's not a choice.
After I choked on food as a kid, I became terrified of eating anything solid. I survived on smoothies and purees for years.
I don't get hungry like other people. I forget to eat and feel full after a few bites. It's exhausting to force myself to meet my calorie needs.
Certain textures make me gag instantly. I can't explain why—it's a physical reaction I can't control.
Treatment helped me slowly expand my safe foods. It was terrifying at first, but now I can eat with friends without panicking.
Learning that my food avoidance was ARFID, not anorexia, was a relief. I never cared about my weight—I just couldn't handle eating.

real_life_examples: A 7-year-old child with extreme texture sensitivities eats only five foods: chicken nuggets, plain pasta, white bread, applesauce, and crackers. Any attempt to introduce new foods results in gagging, crying, and refusal. Growth has faltered, and labs show iron and vitamin D deficiencies. The pediatrician refers to a feeding clinic where an SLP evaluates oral-motor skills (normal) and an OT assesses sensory processing. The family begins CBT-AR with graded exposure: tiny tastes of new foods paired with preferred items, using a reward system. After 12 weeks, the child tolerates 10 additional foods, labs normalize, and mealtime stress decreases significantly.

A 14-year-old develops intense fear of vomiting after a stomach virus and stops eating at school entirely. She loses 15 pounds over 2 months and becomes socially isolated, eating only plain crackers and broth at home. Her parents bring her to a therapist who diagnoses ARFID (fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype). Treatment includes CBT-AR with graded exposure to feared foods, interoceptive exercises, and mirtazapine to reduce nausea anxiety and stimulate appetite. Her pediatrician monitors weight and nutrition. After 4 months, she returns to eating with peers, regains weight, and participates in sports again.

A 22-year-old college student with low appetite and early satiety frequently forgets to eat, relying on meal-replacement shakes to maintain weight. She has no body image concerns but feels full after a few bites and lacks hunger cues. Academic stress worsens the pattern, and she loses 10 pounds. Her doctor diagnoses ARFID (apparent lack of interest subtype) and refers her to a dietitian who creates a structured meal schedule with phone reminders. A therapist teaches her mindfulness and interoceptive awareness to reconnect with hunger signals. ACT-based strategies help her eat for values (energy, social connection) rather than appetite. Over 3 months, her intake and weight stabilize, and she begins enjoying meals with friends.

A 5-year-old with autism eats only beige, crunchy foods (goldfish crackers, french fries, plain chicken) and refuses everything else. He becomes distressed if foods touch each other or if brands change. His weight is stable, but he's diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia and constipation. The family works with an OT trained in feeding therapy, using play-based sensory desensitization (touching, smelling, licking new foods) and differential reinforcement for approach behaviors. Cyproheptadine is added to increase appetite. After 6 months, he accepts 8 new foods, anemia resolves with iron supplementation, and family mealtimes become less stressful.

A 19-year-old male with a history of severe acid reflux avoids most solid foods due to fear of pain and choking. He eats only soft, bland items (oatmeal, yogurt, mashed potatoes) and has lost 20 pounds. GI workup shows well-controlled reflux, but his avoidance persists. He begins CBT-AR targeting the fear-of-aversive-consequences profile. Therapy includes psychoeducation about reflux, graded exposure to previously avoided foods, and anxiety management skills. His GI doctor optimizes reflux treatment. After 5 months of treatment, he reintroduces solid foods, gains weight, and eats out with friends for the first time in years.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve significant food restriction, weight loss, nutritional deficiency, and distress around eating.
comparisons.differences: Anorexia nervosa is driven by fear of weight gain and distorted body image, with overvaluation of thinness. ARFID is driven by sensory sensitivities, fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting), or lack of interest in eating—without body image concerns. Treatment approaches differ significantly.

comparisons.condition: Autism Spectrum Disorder with feeding selectivity
comparisons.similarities: Both can involve sensory sensitivities, rigidity around food routines, and limited food variety.
comparisons.differences: In autism, feeding selectivity may be present but not cause significant nutritional deficiency or psychosocial impairment. ARFID requires that the eating disturbance leads to weight loss, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements/tube feeds, or marked functional interference—severity sufficient to warrant independent clinical attention.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve avoidance of certain foods and distress around eating.
comparisons.differences: Bulimia nervosa centers on binge-purge cycles with overvaluation of weight and shape. ARFID involves restriction without binge eating, purging, or body image concerns. The motivations and treatment approaches are entirely different.

comparisons.condition: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) or other GI disorders
comparisons.similarities: Both can cause food avoidance due to physical discomfort (nausea, pain, reflux).
comparisons.differences: In GERD alone, treating the medical condition typically resolves avoidance. In ARFID, even after GI symptoms are controlled, anxiety and learned avoidance maintain the eating disturbance, requiring behavioral/psychological intervention. ARFID is diagnosed when the eating disturbance exceeds what's expected from the medical condition alone.

faqs.question: Is ARFID just picky eating?
faqs.answer: No. Picky eating is common in childhood and doesn't cause significant nutritional deficiency, weight loss, or functional impairment. ARFID involves severe restriction that leads to medical consequences (malnutrition, reliance on supplements or tube feeds) or marked psychosocial interference (avoiding school, social events). It requires clinical treatment.

faqs.question: Can adults have ARFID?
faqs.answer: Yes. While ARFID often begins in childhood, it can emerge or persist into adolescence and adulthood. Adults with ARFID may have longstanding sensory sensitivities, develop fear-based avoidance after a choking or vomiting event, or have low appetite with difficulty maintaining nutrition. Treatment is available and effective at any age.

faqs.question: How is ARFID different from anorexia nervosa?
faqs.answer: The key difference is motivation. Anorexia nervosa involves restriction driven by fear of weight gain and distorted body image. ARFID involves restriction due to sensory issues, fear of eating consequences (choking, vomiting, pain), or lack of interest in food—without body image concerns. People with ARFID typically don't worry about weight or shape.

faqs.question: What are the three main types of ARFID?
faqs.answer: The three profiles are: 1) Sensory sensitivity (avoidance based on taste, texture, smell, temperature, or appearance); 2) Fear of aversive consequences (fear of choking, vomiting, allergic reaction, or pain); 3) Apparent lack of interest (low appetite, early satiety, forgetting to eat). Many people have a mix of profiles.

faqs.question: Can ARFID be treated?
faqs.answer: Yes. ARFID responds well to evidence-based treatments like CBT-AR (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for ARFID) with graded food exposure, Family-Based Treatment (FBT-ARFID), and feeding therapy with SLP/OT for sensory or oral-motor issues. Nutritional rehabilitation and medical monitoring are also key. Medications can support appetite or reduce anxiety when needed.

faqs.question: Will my child outgrow ARFID?
faqs.answer: Some children improve with development and supportive feeding practices, but many need professional intervention to prevent long-term nutritional and psychosocial consequences. Early treatment improves outcomes and reduces the risk of entrenched patterns. Waiting to 'see if they outgrow it' can lead to worsening deficiencies and anxiety.

faqs.question: What causes ARFID?
faqs.answer: ARFID arises from a combination of factors: sensory processing differences, heightened anxiety or threat perception, genetic predisposition to anxiety or neurodevelopmental traits, adverse feeding experiences (choking, vomiting), and sometimes GI disorders that trigger avoidance. It's not caused by parenting or willful defiance.

faqs.question: Can ARFID occur with autism or ADHD?
faqs.answer: Yes. ARFID is more common in individuals with autism (due to sensory sensitivities and rigidity) and ADHD (due to inattention to hunger cues or impulsivity). However, ARFID is diagnosed separately when the eating disturbance causes significant impairment beyond what's typical for autism or ADHD alone.

faqs.question: What should I do if my child refuses to eat?
faqs.answer: If refusal is acute (sudden, with fever or illness), consult a pediatrician to rule out medical causes. If it's chronic (ongoing, with weight loss, limited variety, or distress), seek evaluation from a feeding specialist or eating disorder professional. Don't force-feed, but do maintain regular meal times and low-pressure exposure to foods with support.

faqs.question: Is tube feeding necessary for ARFID?
faqs.answer: Tube feeding (enteral nutrition) is used when oral intake is insufficient to meet nutritional needs and medical stability is at risk. It's a temporary measure while working on oral intake through therapy. The goal is always to transition back to full oral feeding with graded exposure and support.

faqs.question: Can sensory issues with food be fixed?
faqs.answer: Sensory sensitivities can improve with targeted intervention. Feeding therapy with an SLP or OT uses gradual desensitization and skill-building to increase tolerance of textures, tastes, and smells. CBT-AR also addresses sensory-based avoidance with structured exposure. Progress takes time but is very achievable.

faqs.question: Why do some people with ARFID have no appetite?
faqs.answer: The 'lack of interest' subtype may involve differences in interoceptive awareness (sensing hunger/fullness), altered reward signaling in the brain, or learned patterns of ignoring hunger. Medical causes (medications, GI issues) should be ruled out. Treatment focuses on structured eating schedules and reconnecting with hunger cues.

faqs.question: How long does ARFID treatment take?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some children and adults see improvement in a few months with consistent therapy and family support. Severe cases with longstanding avoidance, sensory defensiveness, or co-occurring anxiety may require 6–12 months or longer. Early intervention and treatment adherence speed recovery.

faqs.question: Can ARFID cause long-term health problems?
faqs.answer: Untreated ARFID can lead to malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies (iron, zinc, vitamin D), growth delays in children, low bone density, delayed puberty, weakened immune function, and social isolation. Early treatment prevents or reverses most complications and supports healthy development.

faqs.question: What is graded exposure for ARFID?
faqs.answer: Graded exposure is a core ARFID treatment technique where feared or avoided foods are introduced in tiny, manageable steps—starting with looking at or touching the food, then smelling, licking, taking small bites, and eventually eating full portions. Each step is practiced repeatedly until anxiety decreases before moving to the next. It's done in a supportive, non-pressuring way.

faqs.question: Can medications help with ARFID?
faqs.answer: Medications don't cure ARFID but can support treatment. Cyproheptadine (especially in children) and mirtazapine stimulate appetite and reduce nausea/anxiety. SSRIs help with comorbid anxiety or OCD. Ondansetron can reduce fear of vomiting short-term. Medication is always combined with therapy and nutritional rehabilitation.

faqs.question: Is ARFID related to anxiety disorders?
faqs.answer: Yes, ARFID often co-occurs with anxiety disorders, especially in the fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype. Anxiety about choking, vomiting, or pain maintains avoidance. Treatment targets both the eating disturbance and underlying anxiety using exposure therapy, relaxation skills, and sometimes medication.

faqs.question: What should parents do during meals?
faqs.answer: Create a low-pressure environment: offer foods without forcing, praise approach behaviors (touching, smelling, trying), avoid battles or bribes, keep meals at consistent times, and model relaxed eating. Work with a therapist or feeding specialist to develop a tailored plan. Consistency and patience are key.

faqs.question: Can ARFID start after a traumatic event?
faqs.answer: Yes. Choking, severe vomiting, anaphylaxis, or other frightening experiences can trigger fear-based ARFID. The avoidance becomes conditioned and persists even after the event is over. Treatment focuses on gradually re-exposing the person to feared foods in a safe, controlled way to reduce anxiety.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ARFID and orthorexia?
faqs.answer: Orthorexia (not a formal DSM diagnosis) involves obsession with 'healthy' or 'pure' eating, often with moral judgments about food and rigidity around diet quality. ARFID involves avoidance due to sensory issues, fear, or lack of interest—not moral or health-focused beliefs. The motivations and treatment approaches differ.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek evaluation if food avoidance leads to weight loss/faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, reliance on supplements/tube feeds, or marked interference with school/work/social life. Urgent medical care is needed for syncope, bradycardia, or electrolyte abnormalities.

positive_factors: Readiness for graded exposure and skills practice
Effective management of GI symptoms and anxiety
challenging_factors: Severe sensory defensiveness or traumatic feeding history
Long duration of restricted diet with entrenched routines
Co-occurring ASD/OCD with rigidity and high anxiety without tailored supports

tiles.title: What is ARFID?
tiles.summary: Food restriction due to sensory issues, fear of consequences, or low appetite—not body image concerns.

tiles.title: Signs & Symptoms
tiles.summary: Limited food variety, sensory sensitivities, fear of choking or vomiting, low appetite, and nutritional deficiencies.

tiles.title: Causes & Risk Factors
tiles.summary: Sensory processing differences, anxiety, adverse feeding experiences, autism, ADHD, and GI issues.

tiles.title: How It's Diagnosed
tiles.summary: Feeding history, growth assessment, lab work, sensory evaluation, and ruling out anorexia or medical causes.

tiles.title: Treatment Options
tiles.summary: CBT-AR with graded exposure, Family-Based Treatment, feeding therapy, nutritional rehabilitation, and medications.

tiles.title: Medical Complications
tiles.summary: Malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, growth delays, low bone density, and social isolation.

tiles.title: Recovery & Prognosis
tiles.summary: Good outcomes with early intervention. Graded exposure and family support lead to food variety expansion.

tiles.title: Living with ARFID
tiles.summary: Structured meals, low-pressure exposure, managing anxiety, family support, and school accommodations.

tiles.title: Getting Help
tiles.summary: Seek evaluation for significant food avoidance, weight loss, nutritional deficiency, or feeding tube dependence.
